interviewQuestions.question: Why would a serverless function benefit from a native image over a JIT'd runtime?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It comes down to whether the workload lives long enough to earn back a JIT's warm-up cost, and a serverless function usually doesn't. A JVM cold start pays for classloading, heap setup, and interpreted execution — commonly 100–300ms — before the tiered JIT has compiled anything, and a sparse-traffic function can pay that cost on every single invocation if the platform doesn't keep an instance warm.

A GraalVM native-image binary is compiled fully to native code ahead of time, so there's no classloading step and no interpreter ramp — it starts executing at whatever speed the build-time compiler could produce, typically single-digit to low tens of milliseconds. For a function billed per invocation and judged on cold-start latency, that difference is the whole story.

The trade I'd name explicitly: native-image gives up the JIT's ability to adapt to real traffic patterns over time, and it needs reflection/dynamic class loading declared ahead of build via configuration — a real migration cost for reflection-heavy frameworks. For a function that's genuinely short-lived, that trade is easy; for a long-running service that would actually benefit from profile-guided optimization, I'd keep the JVM and its JIT instead.

**Testing:** whether you connect the AOT benefit to the specific workload shape (short-lived, cold-start-sensitive) rather than treating AOT as a universal upgrade.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the 'closed-world assumption' in GraalVM native-image, and what does it break in a typical Spring application?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
It means the native-image build tool has to see the program's entire reachable call graph at build time — every class that might be loaded, every method that might be called — because anything not in that graph simply won't exist in the compiled binary. There's no JIT standing by to compile a surprise path at runtime the way a normal JVM would.

This breaks a lot of what makes frameworks like Spring convenient by default: dependency injection frameworks routinely load classes by name from configuration, generate proxy classes at runtime for AOP/interception, and use reflection heavily to wire beans together — all decisions the framework normally makes *while running*, which the closed-world assumption requires knowing in advance instead.

The practical fix isn't avoiding these frameworks — it's using their native-image-aware modes: Spring's AOT processing (introduced specifically for this) precomputes the bean graph and generates the reflection configuration at build time instead of discovering it at runtime, and a build-time agent can trace a representative run of the app to auto-generate the rest of the configuration. Miss a reflectively-accessed class the agent didn't see during tracing, and it fails at runtime with no fallback — which is why native-image migrations lean heavily on integration test coverage during the tracing run.

**Testing:** whether you can connect an abstract constraint (closed-world assumption) to a concrete, common framework pattern it breaks.

interviewQuestions.question: Is it fair to say Go and Rust binaries have 'no runtime' the way a compiled native-image Java binary does?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Not quite — I'd push back on the framing before agreeing with it. "No runtime" usually means "no separate persistent VM process interpreting or JIT-compiling bytecode," and that part is true for both: there's no equivalent of a JVM sitting there deciding what to compile next. But that's different from "no runtime code at all."

Go statically links a scheduler and a garbage collector directly into every compiled binary — there's no external Go VM, but there is real runtime code executing goroutine scheduling and GC cycles inside your process the whole time it runs. Rust is closer to the "genuinely minimal" end: its ownership and borrow-checking (covered in `ownership-and-borrowing`) happens entirely at compile time, so a compiled Rust binary has essentially no runtime memory-management code running — no GC, no scheduler unless you explicitly bring in an async runtime like Tokio.

A GraalVM native-image Java binary sits in between: it's AOT-compiled like Go and Rust, but the resulting binary still embeds a GC and other JVM-derived runtime services, because Java's memory model was built around having a GC — you can't compile that requirement away, only compile *when* the code that implements it runs.

So the accurate statement is: all three skip the *separate persistent VM* model, but differ substantially in how much runtime machinery is still statically linked into the binary itself.

**Testing:** whether you resist an oversimplified claim and can distinguish 'no VM process' from 'no runtime code whatsoever.'

interviewQuestions.question: Your team's Java service currently on the JVM is considering a native-image migration purely to reduce cold-start latency. What would you check before committing to it?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
First, I'd confirm cold start is actually the bottleneck worth solving — if the service runs as a long-lived container that stays warm, native-image trades away the JIT's steady-state throughput advantage for a cold-start win that container warm-keeping might already give you for free. I'd check the actual invocation pattern (serverless-style scale-to-zero vs always-on) before assuming AOT is the right lever.

Second, I'd audit reflection and dynamic-class-loading usage across the codebase and its dependencies — dependency injection frameworks, ORMs doing runtime proxy generation, and any bytecode manipulation libraries are the highest-risk areas. I'd specifically check whether the frameworks in use ship a native-image-aware mode (Spring AOT, Micronaut, Quarkus) versus needing hand-written reflection configuration, since the latter is a real, ongoing maintenance cost every time a new reflective path gets added.

Third, I'd run the build-time tracing agent against representative integration test coverage — not just unit tests — since any reflective path the agent never observes during tracing will fail silently at runtime with no JIT fallback to catch it. Weak integration test coverage is a bigger native-image migration risk than most teams expect going in.

Finally, I'd benchmark both the build time (native-image builds can take minutes, a real CI cost) and the actual measured cold-start improvement before committing — the theoretical benefit is well-documented, but the specific numbers for *this* codebase's dependency graph are what should decide it.

**Testing:** whether you can turn a strategic direction into a concrete, risk-ordered technical audit rather than assuming the migration is straightforward.
